title: DoorDash
seoTitle: Design a Food Delivery Platform like DoorDash
description: Design a global food delivery platform like DoorDash — restaurant search by location, ordering, dispatching orders to couriers, live courier tracking, and ETA prediction across many cities.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is DoorDash?
blocks.text: DoorDash, Uber Eats and Deliveroo connect three parties: **customers** who order food, **restaurants** that prepare it, and **couriers** (Dashers) who pick it up and deliver it. The system has to show what's available nearby, take orders, choose the right courier at the right moment so food isn't left waiting, and track delivery live — in hundreds of cities worldwide.

items: Customers should be able to browse restaurants that deliver to their location, with menus and estimated delivery times.
Customers should be able to place and pay for an order.
Restaurants should receive orders and mark them as ready.
The system should assign each order to a courier, who can accept or decline.
Customers should be able to track their courier live.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: An order is never assigned to two couriers at once.
Courier locations update every few seconds, with high write volume.
Scale to ~1M orders per hour at dinner peak and ~1M active couriers globally.
Regional isolation: an outage in one region shouldn't affect others.
Strong consistency for menus (minutes of staleness is fine).
**Restaurant**: location, delivery radius or zone, hours, menu, current prep-time estimate.
**Order**: customer, restaurant, items, status (`placed`, `confirmed`, `ready`, `picked_up`, `delivered`), assigned courier.
**Delivery offer**: an order offered to a courier, with expiry.

blocks.code:
GET  /restaurants?lat=&lng=&cuisine= -> [{ restaurant, etaMinutes }]
POST /orders { restaurantId, items[], address, paymentMethodId, idempotencyKey }
POST /restaurant/orders/:id/ready
PUT  /couriers/me/location { lat, lng, ts }          (every ~4s)
POST /couriers/me/offers/:id/accept | decline
WS   /orders/:id/track -> courier location + status

blocks.text: Restaurants are indexed by **geohash/H3 cell**. A query takes the customer's cell and neighbouring cells, filters by open hours and delivery zone, and ranks by relevance and ETA. Menus and restaurant pages are cached heavily since they change rarely.

The **Order Service** validates items and prices, charges via the payment service (idempotent), stores the order and sends it to the restaurant's tablet. The order then moves through a state machine driven by events.

Couriers' locations stream into a **Location Service** that keeps the latest position per courier in an in-memory geo index (Redis GEO or H3 buckets). The **Dispatch Service** finds available couriers near the restaurant, picks the best one, and sends an **offer** with a short expiry. On accept, the order is assigned; on decline or timeout, the next candidate is offered.
The tracking service subscribes to the assigned courier's location updates and pushes them to the customer over a **WebSocket** or SSE, along with status changes.
1) When and to whom should we dispatch?

approach.text: As soon as an order is placed, offer it to the closest available courier.

challenges.text: The courier arrives long before the food is ready and waits, wasting capacity, while orders placed a minute later might have suited them better.

approach.text: Predict when the food will be ready (per-restaurant prep-time model) and dispatch so the courier's travel time ends just as the food is ready.

challenges.text: Still greedy: each order is matched in isolation.

approach.text: Every few seconds, for each geographic zone, solve an **assignment problem** over all pending orders and available couriers, minimising expected delivery time and courier idle time using predicted prep times and travel times. Allow **batching** two orders from the same or nearby restaurants to one courier. Offers go out from the solution, and declines feed back into the next round.

challenges.text: Needs accurate ETA models and enough compute per zone at peak, with a greedy fallback if the solver is late.

blocks.text: 2) How do we avoid assigning an order to two couriers?

Offers are sent one at a time per order with an expiry, and acceptance is a **conditional update**: `UPDATE orders SET courier = ? WHERE id = ? AND courier IS NULL AND status = 'awaiting_courier'`. If two couriers somehow accept, only one update succeeds; the other gets "no longer available". Couriers are similarly locked so they can't accept two incompatible offers.
Mention the unhappy paths: a courier who goes offline mid-delivery triggers re-dispatch, and a restaurant that runs late shifts the dispatch time.
3) How do we handle 1M couriers sending locations every 4 seconds?

That's ~250k writes per second. Location updates go to the Location Service, which keeps only the **latest point in memory**, sharded by city or region, and streams updates to Kafka for tracking, ETAs and analytics. Nothing is written to a relational database per update. Each region runs its own stack (location, dispatch, orders) so a failure stays local, with global services only for accounts and payments.

quiz.question: Why not dispatch the nearest courier immediately?
options: The courier may wait a long time for food that isn't ready
quiz.explanation: Dispatch timing should match predicted prep time.

quiz.question: How do we ensure one courier per order?
options: A conditional update that only assigns if no courier is set
quiz.explanation: The database guarantees only one acceptance wins.

quiz.question: How should courier location updates be stored?
options: A row per update in SQL
Latest position in an in-memory geo index, history streamed to Kafka
quiz.explanation: Only the latest location is needed for dispatch.

quiz.question: Why run separate regional stacks?
options: To keep failures and latency local to each region
quiz.explanation: Orders and couriers in one city rarely interact with another.
